lesson.title: Cognitivism, humanism and psychoanalysis
lesson.summary: Contemporary psychology inherited traditions that neither ask the same questions nor apply the same standards of evidence. This lesson presents the cognitive revolution, the humanistic approach and the psychoanalytic or psychodynamic tradition while distinguishing historical contribution, concepts, testable predictions and empirical scope.
objectives: Explain how the cognitive revolution made mental processes compatible with experimental study.
Present the central questions of the humanistic approach without treating its values as demonstrated findings.
Distinguish historical Freudian psychoanalysis from later psychodynamic approaches.
Compare several traditions through their mechanisms, predictions and levels of evidence.
prerequisites: Distinguish observable behaviour from a mental process.
Understand the behaviorist project and the principles of conditioning.

content.text: From the 1950s, work in psychology, linguistics, computer science and neuroscience renewed the study of memory, language, attention and problem solving. The cognitive revolution was not simply a return to free introspection: it built information-processing models and tested them against observable responses, errors, reaction times and recall performance. A mental process can therefore be theorised without being treated as directly visible.

Two people obtain the same score on a memory task, but one answers quickly with some errors while the other answers slowly without errors. A cognitive model can propose different strategies, then predict how performance will change if the delay, load or instruction varies. The model is useful if it produces predictions that could fail, not merely if it tells a plausible story after the event.

The humanistic approach developed in reaction to views of behaviour and personality considered overly deterministic. It emphasises lived experience, meaning, choice, relationships and personal growth. Carl Rogers notably emphasised a person-centred relationship. These orientations influenced clinical practice and ideas about the therapeutic alliance, but their values, personality models and the effects of an intervention must be evaluated separately.

Freudian psychoanalysis proposes that unconscious conflicts and processes contribute to behaviour and personality. Its historical influence on psychotherapy, culture and attention to personal history is substantial. Several classical propositions are nevertheless difficult to falsify or have received limited direct support. Later psychodynamic approaches changed concepts, duration and methods; evaluating them requires distinguishing a general theory, a precise mechanism and the effectiveness of a defined intervention.

Key point: comparing traditions means neither choosing a school as an identity nor declaring them equally supported. For the same case, specify the question, proposed mechanism, expected observations, alternative explanations and available level of evidence. Ideas from different traditions can be reformulated and tested without validating their entire historical system.

concepts.title: The cognitive revolution
concepts.description: The cognitive revolution restored the study of representations and mental processes through models that generate observable predictions.

concepts.title: The humanistic perspective
concepts.description: The humanistic approach emphasises lived experience, meaning, relationships and capacity for growth while requiring values to be distinguished from empirical claims.

concepts.title: Psychoanalysis and psychodynamic approaches
concepts.description: Historical psychoanalysis and psychodynamic approaches give a role to unconscious processes and relational history, but their propositions and interventions must be evaluated separately.

assessment.title: Concept check — Psychoanalysis and psychodynamic approaches

tasks.description: Using the humanistic section, create three columns: value or priority, proposition about human functioning, and observation needed to evaluate it.

tasks.title: Compare four explanations of the same case
tasks.description: For a person postponing an important task, formulate a behaviorist, cognitive, humanistic and psychodynamic hypothesis; for each, state one prediction, one useful datum and one limitation.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a scientific cognitive explanation from a plausible story told after the event?
questions.explanation: A scientific model makes observable predictions that can be contradicted.

questions.prompt: Which measurements can test a cognitive model?
questions.explanation: Time, errors and recall are observable indicators that allow the model to be compared with data.

questions.prompt: The cognitive revolution made observable behaviour unnecessary.
questions.explanation: Cognitive models are tested precisely through observable responses and performance.

questions.prompt: Which context contributed to the cognitive revolution?
questions.explanation: Developments in linguistics, computer science, neuroscience and psychology renewed the study of the mind.

options.label: Exchange among several disciplines in the 1950s
The disappearance of memory as a subject
An exclusive return to ancient philosophy

questions.prompt: What is the movement that restored the scientific study of mental processes to a central place from the 1950s called?
Which theme is central to the humanistic approach?
questions.explanation: Lived experience, meaning, relationships and potential for growth occupy a central place.

options.label: Explaining every behaviour through one gene

questions.prompt: A humanistic value and a claim about therapeutic effectiveness are validated in exactly the same way.
questions.explanation: A value guides practice; a claim about effects requires a defined empirical evaluation.

questions.prompt: Which psychologist is most associated with the person-centred approach?
questions.explanation: Carl Rogers developed the person-centred approach.

questions.prompt: What must be distinguished when evaluating a humanistic proposition?
questions.explanation: Clarity requires separating values, theoretical models and observable effects of an intervention.

options.label: The idea that all claims are equivalent

questions.prompt: Which humanistic psychologist is associated with the hierarchy of needs and self-actualisation?

questions.prompt: Which distinction is most important when evaluating the psychodynamic tradition?
questions.explanation: A historical theory, a precise mechanism and a defined intervention do not automatically have the same support.

options.label: Distinguish the historical system, mechanism and intervention
Confuse cultural influence with experimental evidence

questions.prompt: The historical influence of a theory is sufficient to demonstrate all its propositions.
questions.explanation: Historical influence and empirical support are distinct questions.

questions.prompt: Which themes belong to the psychoanalytic or psychodynamic tradition?
questions.explanation: This tradition notably emphasises unconscious processes, conflicts and relational history.

questions.prompt: Why are some classical Freudian propositions difficult to evaluate scientifically?
questions.explanation: They may be framed so that they explain opposing results without a clear observation capable of refuting them.

options.label: They sometimes lack explicit falsification criteria
They always use measurements that are too precise
